Clinical Vignette: Martin

Martin is a 56-year-old married man of Dutch origin who has spent most of his adult life as a professional musician — a session guitarist who has worked steadily across recording studios and small concert venues for nearly three decades. He describes his relationship with music as the one constant in his life, the place where he has always felt most himself. That sense of safety, he says quietly, is something he is no longer sure he can find anywhere.

Eighteen months ago, Martin was sexually assaulted by a trusted colleague — a producer he had worked with for years — following a late-night session at a private studio. He had stayed behind to finish overdubs. They were alone. What happened that night, he says, came from someone he never imagined capable of it, and that betrayal sits alongside the assault itself as a wound he cannot seem to close. He did not report it. He drove home in the early hours, showered, and told his wife he was tired. He has never used the word "assault" with her, though she knows something is wrong.

In the weeks that followed, Martin functioned on the surface. He took bookings, showed up to sessions, played the notes. But he began to notice that certain sounds — a particular type of ambient studio reverb, the smell of a specific brand of cigarette the producer smoked — would pull him back into that room with a violence that left him gripping the edge of whatever surface was nearest. He describes these intrusions as not quite memories, more like being physically dragged backward in time. His body, he says, does not seem to understand that it is over.

Sleep has become a negotiation he rarely wins. He wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, heart pounding, certain that something is in the room. His wife reaches for him and he flinches before he can stop himself. He has begun sleeping on the couch, telling her his insomnia disturbs her rest. The distance between them has grown in ways neither of them has found the language to address.

Martin has quietly restructured his professional life around avoidance. He no longer takes private studio sessions. He turns down work that requires him to be alone with a male producer or engineer. He has manufactured excuses — scheduling conflicts, a hand injury — that have cost him relationships and income he cannot easily replace. What troubles him most, he admits, is that he used to walk into a studio and feel the tension leave his shoulders. Now he scans every room before he enters it, noting exits, calculating distances, reading the body language of every man present.

He carries a low, grinding shame that he finds almost impossible to articulate. He is fifty-six years old. He is, in his own words, not someone this happens to. He has spent months constructing arguments for why his response is disproportionate, why he should simply move past it, and then finding himself unable to get out of his car in a studio car park, hands shaking on the steering wheel. He is irritable in ways that frighten him — snapping at his wife over small things, feeling a surge of cold rage when he is startled, then sitting afterward with a self-disgust he cannot shake.

Music, the thing that has organized his interior life since adolescence, has become complicated in a way he grieves deeply. He still plays — he cannot imagine not playing — but there are sessions where he watches his own hands on the fretboard as though they belong to someone else, and the sound he produces feels like it is coming from a great distance. He describes sitting alone one evening with his guitar and realizing he had played the same four bars for forty minutes without registering a single note.

Martin presents as a man who is quietly exhausted by the effort of holding himself together, and who has only recently begun to consider that holding himself together may not, in fact, be the same as healing.
